analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicaid, Medicare, and private insurers to cover annual lung cancer screenings without prior authorization or cost sharing.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill has drawn two Democratic sponsors and no action since; it authorizes $10 million a year in screening outreach.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require Medicaid to cover annual lung cancer scans for everyone the official screening guidelines recommend, with no copays and no prior-authorization step, starting in 2028. It would bar Medicare Advantage plans and private insurers from requiring prior authorization for those scans. It would also expand Medicaid coverage of counseling and medications to quit smoking to all enrollees, not just pregnant women, and include e-cigarettes and vape pens. A public outreach campaign and a government study on who is getting lung cancer and who is getting screened round out the bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Smokers and former smokers who fall in the recommended screening group (people at high risk based on the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force guidelines in place as of March 9, 2021), especially Medicaid enrollees, who today can face copays and prior-authorization delays. Medicaid enrollees who want to quit smoking also gain guaranteed coverage of counseling and cessation medications, including vaping products.

how_it_helps.text: Medicaid must cover annual lung cancer screening for guideline-eligible individuals with no cost sharing and without regard to prior authorization, effective January 1, 2028.
Medicare and Medicare Advantage plans, as well as group and individual private health plans, may not impose prior authorization on annual lung cancer screening for people the guidelines recommend.
Medicaid coverage of tobacco-cessation counseling and pharmacotherapy is expanded from pregnant women only to all enrollees, explicitly including e-cigarettes and vape pens.
Medicaid managed care contracts must require coverage of both the screening and cessation services without prior authorization.

The Department of Health and Human Services would run a targeted outreach campaign on who should be screened, funded at $10 million a year for fiscal years 2028 through 2032, and the Government Accountability Office would report on who is diagnosed with lung cancer but falls outside current screening guidelines, such as firefighters, veterans, and women under 50.

analysis.who_pays: If it passes, the cost falls on the federal government and states, which share Medicaid financing, and on private insurance premiums, since plans must cover the screenings and cessation services without gatekeeping. Insurers also lose the prior-authorization control they use to manage imaging spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, state Medicaid budgets, and insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new federal coverage mandates on state Medicaid programs and on employer and individual private plans, effective in 2028, and states must fit the requirements into their existing Medicaid plans.
The outreach campaign would cost $10 million a year for five years, spent from federal appropriations.
Removing prior authorization for screening scans removes a utilization check insurers use to manage imaging volume and spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people in the screening guidelines' target group, the gains are concrete: removing prior authorization and Medicaid copays makes it easier to get a scan that catches lung cancer earlier, when treatment works best. The main honest costs are money — higher federal and state Medicaid spending and somewhat higher premiums — and a medical tradeoff: widespread CT screening produces false positives that can lead to follow-up scans and biopsies on people who do not have cancer. The bill tries to limit that by pegging eligibility to the official task force guidelines as of March 2021, though it locks those guidelines in place and only allows them to broaden, not narrow.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in May 2026, read twice, and sent to the Finance Committee, which has not acted on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on May 19, 2026, with Sen. Hirono joining.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action, hearing, or vote has occurred; the bill sits with one cosponsor among the Senate's 45 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved on the bill, which means insurers keep their prior-authorization gatekeeping over lung cancer screening and Medicaid enrollees get none of the new coverage. The companies that would gain new screening and cessation business have not gained it yet either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers keep screening gatekeeping, for now

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on May 19, 2026.

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral; has taken no action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 19, 2026 and has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No one has opposed it on the record, but its only support is Democratic — Durbin and one of the Senate's 45 Democrats — in a chamber where Republicans hold 55 seats, so it has not yet faced a real test.

industries.industry: Health insurers (Medicaid managed care, Medicare Advantage, and private plans)
industries.note: The bill strips these plans of prior-authorization control over lung cancer screening and, in Medicaid, of cost sharing, cutting into the utilization management tools they use to limit imaging spending. Patients get the scan without a middleman delay.

industries.industry: Medical imaging providers, hospitals, and radiology practices
industries.note: Guaranteed coverage without prior authorization means more screening CT scans reach eligible patients faster, and providers get paid without fighting insurer denials.

industries.industry: Tobacco-cessation treatment makers (nicotine replacement and other cessation drugs)
industries.note: Medicaid must cover counseling and cessation pharmacotherapy for all enrollees, including e-cigarettes and vape pens, creating a larger guaranteed customer base for these products.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee with two Democratic sponsors and no Republican support in a 55-seat Republican majority. Bills at this stage with this level of sponsorship almost never reach the floor on their own; its realistic path is being folded into a larger health package, which is unlikely this session.
